title: Training with ML-labeled Data via Stochastic First- and Zeroth-Order Optimization
authors: Maria-Eleni Sfyraki, Jun-Kun Wang
abstract: Training a machine learning (ML) model is an optimization process that typically requires a set of examples with ground-truth labels beforehand. Obtaining these ground truths usually requires laborious human effort and can be costly. The scalability of human labeling becomes a concern when there are a large number of data points that need to be labeled. To address this practical issue, we consider an optimization setting where a subset of samples has ground-truth labels, while the remaining data points were labeled by an ML predictor, which could potentially assign incorrect labels to those points. We propose both first-order and zeroth-order stochastic optimization methods for training on datasets consisting of a mix of true-labeled and ML-labeled samples. We further conduct comprehensive empirical studies from training a linear regression model to fine-tuning a large language model (LLM) to showcase the effectiveness of the proposed algorithms for training with ML-labeled data.

infographic.key_insight: The paper proposes stochastic first- and zeroth-order optimization methods for training on a mix of ground-truth and potentially incorrect ML-generated labels.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These methods target scalable model training when human labeling is costly and only part of a dataset has ground-truth labels.
method: Combine ground-truth-labeled samples with ML-labeled samples.
Develop stochastic first-order optimization methods for mixed-label training.
Develop stochastic zeroth-order alternatives for the same setting.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports empirical studies ranging from linear regression training to LLM fine-tuning, but provides no quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: Sensitivity to ML-label error rates and patterns should be checked before deployment; the abstract does not specify robustness limits.
infographic.paper_title: Training with ML-labeled Data via Stochastic First- and Zeroth-Order Optimization

title: HarnessPro: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement with Pareto Optimization for Performance-Cost Trade-offs
authors: Zhuoshi Pan, ZhiYuan Feng, Yukuo Cen, Honglin Lin, Junru Lu, Zhongxia Chen
abstract: Harness development plays a crucial role in building capable AI agents. Recent approaches improve harnesses through recursive self-improvement (RSI), but their performance gains often come with higher execution costs. We introduce HarnessPro, a label-free method for evolving harnesses to improve task performance while reducing execution cost. In this setting, candidate harnesses are evaluated using LLM-generated tests without access to ground-truth solutions or official tests. Specialized agents diagnose execution trajectories, plan updates with different performance-cost priorities, and implement them as candidate harnesses. Rather than returning a single harness, HarnessPro uses normalized weighted squared-distance selection to provide cost-focused (lite), balanced (medium), and performance-focused (heavy) harnesses for different deployment budgets. Selected harnesses enter the next iteration, where execution feedback guides further updates. Our experiments cover Terminal-Bench 2, SWE-Bench Pro, and ProgramBench, using GPT-5.5 with Codex and GLM-5.2 with Claude Code. Across these benchmarks using GPT-5.5 with Codex, the heavy mode of HarnessPro achieves an average pass-rate gain of 2.0 percentage points and an average per-task cost reduction of 26.1% relative to RHO. This advantage also holds when using GLM-5.2 with Claude Code. Code is available at https://github.com/pzs19/HarnessPro

infographic.key_insight: HarnessPro recursively improves AI-agent harnesses to offer performance–cost trade-offs, with its heavy mode outperforming RHO while reducing execution cost.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Engineers can select lite, medium, or heavy harnesses to match deployment budgets rather than optimize task success alone.
method: Evaluate candidate harnesses with LLM-generated tests, without ground-truth solutions or official tests.
Use specialized agents to diagnose execution traces, plan performance–cost updates, and implement candidates.
Select lite, medium, and heavy variants using normalized weighted squared distance, then iterate with execution feedback.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across Terminal-Bench 2, SWE-Bench Pro, and ProgramBench with GPT-5.5 and Codex, heavy mode averages a 2.0-percentage-point pass-rate gain and 26.1% lower per-task cost versus RHO; the abstract also reports an advantage with GLM-5.2 and Claude Code.
infographic.watch_item: LLM-generated tests may miss real task requirements, so label-free optimization needs independent validation before deployment.
infographic.paper_title: HarnessPro: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement with Pareto Optimization for Performance-Cost Trade-offs

title: PACT: Plan-Augmented Coordination via Trace-Graphs for Dynamic Multi-Agent Combinatorial Optimization
authors: Xiao Zhou, Alex Schutz, Victor-Alexandru Darvariu, Nick Hawes
abstract: Multi-agent approaches have been investigated recently as a means of improving the scalability of reinforcement learning for neural combinatorial optimization. Existing methods assume that all problem instance information is known upfront. However, real-world problems are often dynamic: relevant information is progressively revealed as the agents take actions (e.g., arriving at an edge in a routing problem only to discover it is untraversable). In such cases, existing methods fail to coordinate agents to explore and exploit the progressively revealed information. To address the arising coordination challenge, we introduce PACT (Plan-Augmented Coordination via Trace-graphs). PACT augments the environment graph with auxiliary nodes representing the plans of agents, which are connected to the resource nodes to indicate future dependencies. The proposed message-passing scheme over the augmented graph grounds inter-agent coordination in the environment and enables proactive, rather than reactive, conflict resolution. We show that PACT improves solution quality in dynamic problems relative to baselines and exhibits the best transfer to larger instances on which, remarkably, it outperforms centralized oracles with privileged access to instance uncertainty.

infographic.key_insight: PACT coordinates agents in dynamic combinatorial optimization by representing their plans in a shared graph, enabling proactive conflict resolution as information is revealed.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could improve multi-agent routing and resource allocation when agents must coordinate under progressively revealed constraints.
method: Augment the environment graph with auxiliary nodes representing agent plans.
Connect plan nodes to resource nodes to encode future dependencies.
Use message passing over the augmented graph to support inter-agent coordination.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports better solution quality than baselines on dynamic problems and the best transfer to larger instances, where PACT outperforms centralized oracles with privileged access to instance uncertainty.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify graph-construction or message-passing overhead, leaving deployment scalability unclear.
infographic.paper_title: PACT: Plan-Augmented Coordination via Trace-Graphs for Dynamic Multi-Agent Combinatorial Optimization

title: Cross-Fitting for Neural Posterior Estimation
authors: Jeffrey Regier
abstract: Neural Posterior Estimation (NPE) fits an amortized conditional density estimator to a simulated training set of complete-data realizations. NPE's training objective, log-likelihood, favors posterior approximations that assign arbitrarily high density to the training points, and typical families of amortized conditional density estimators (e.g., normalizing flows, Gaussian encoders) are flexible enough to oblige. The resulting policy of extreme overconfidence translates poorly to held-out data. Early stopping and other regularizers can prevent this degeneracy, but they are limited to selecting posterior approximations along an unfavorable optimization trajectory set by in-sample residuals, where the posterior mean is underfit while the posterior variance is overfit. To avoid this trade-off, we propose Cross-Fitting NPE (CF-NPE), which uses sample splitting to separate conditional-mean estimation from the estimation of the posterior's higher moments. Using $K$-fold cross-fitting, CF-NPE fits $K$ posterior-mean regressors and then fits a conditional density estimator to the resulting out-of-fold residuals. In experiments with synthetic data and in a cosmological application, CF-NPE achieves higher held-out log-likelihood than standard NPE and typically improves calibration. CF-NPE is most useful in high-dimensional, simulation-limited settings.

infographic.key_insight: Cross-Fitting NPE separates posterior-mean learning from residual-density learning to reduce the overconfidence caused by fitting both on the same training samples.
infographic.engineering_relevance: CF-NPE can improve uncertainty estimates for simulation-based inference, especially when parameters are high-dimensional and simulations are limited.
method: Split simulated parameter–observation pairs into K folds.
Train K posterior-mean regressors and compute out-of-fold residuals.
Fit a conditional density estimator to those residuals to model uncertainty around the estimated mean.
infographic.evidence_signal: On synthetic data and a cosmological application, CF-NPE achieves higher held-out log-likelihood than standard NPE and typically improves calibration.
infographic.watch_item: Training K mean regressors adds computational overhead, and calibration gains are not guaranteed in every setting.
infographic.paper_title: Cross-Fitting for Neural Posterior Estimation

title: Same Simulation, Different Evidence: Where Retrieved Tool Output Costs LLM Agents Accuracy
authors: Ke Zhang, Sahchit Chundur, Jerry Peprah Owusu, Mohammad Javad Abdolhosseini Qomi, Maziar Raissi
abstract: LLM agents that compute the right answer can still answer wrongly. Agent harnesses increasingly keep long tool outputs out of the context window, saving them to files that the agent searches or reads on demand. We ask where this costs accuracy with a real scientific tool: PHREEQC, a widely used geochemistry simulator from the USGS, whose reports reach 846.8k characters and whose determinism lets every printed value be traced. Agents use it to answer 158 execution-verified multiple-choice items. When agents read the simulator's report through a section index rather than in context, GPT-5.1 and GPT-5.2 lose 11.3 and 7.9 points of accuracy, while Claude Opus 4.6 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 show no detectable cost. Re-running all 11,007 logged simulator calls shows that both GPT models compute the keyed value about as often as before; what changes is the evidence they answer from. Under retrieval they often skip the report, answer from their own higher-precision output files, and misround to a neighboring option, a failure we call evidence substitution. With the simulation held fixed, retrieval still costs GPT-5.2 9.4 points. For GPT-5.4, more frequent correct simulations mask an evidence-use loss of about ten points, leaving a net change indistinguishable from zero. Naming the authoritative output raises accuracy by 6.3-7.9 points over plain retrieval for the three GPT models; for GPT-5.1 and GPT-5.2, inlining outputs that fit works as well, while asking for correct rounding does not. Context-management choices in agent harnesses should be judged by where accuracy is lost, not only by final accuracy.

infographic.key_insight: LLM agents can run the correct simulation yet answer incorrectly when retrieved tool reports are replaced by non-authoritative evidence.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Scientific agent harnesses should identify authoritative outputs and evaluate evidence use separately from simulation correctness.
method: Evaluated agents on 158 execution-verified multiple-choice questions using the deterministic PHREEQC geochemistry simulator.
Compared in-context reports with section-index retrieval and replayed 11,007 logged simulator calls.
Tested fixed-simulation comparisons, authoritative-output guidance, inlining, and rounding instructions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Section-index retrieval reduced GPT-5.1 and GPT-5.2 accuracy by 11.3 and 7.9 percentage points, respectively, while neither Claude model showed a detectable cost.
infographic.watch_item: Effects vary by model, and unchanged final accuracy can conceal evidence-use losses offset by more frequent correct simulations.
infographic.paper_title: Same Simulation, Different Evidence: Where Retrieved Tool Output Costs LLM Agents Accuracy

title: Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Market Making on Prediction-Market Order Books
authors: Skander Lejmi
abstract: A market maker provides liquidity by quoting prices to buy and sell an asset, earning the spread while managing inventory risk. We study market makers trained with multi-agent reinforcement learning on prediction markets, specifically Polymarket, whose thin order books pose distinct challenges. Three challenges underpin this research: adverse selection may cause a policy trained on real data to stop quoting; the consequences of a quote can arrive many steps after the action; and prediction-market L2 data does not identify individual orders needed for simulation. We address these challenges by reconstructing order-level LOBSTER-format data from Polymarket and training agents in JaxMARL-HFT on 417 real markets. We enrich the baseline market maker's observation space with the book and recent flow, redesign its actions and inventory controls, and propose a cooperative multi-agent decomposition into a quoter and a risk manager trained using recurrent Independent Proximal Policy Optimisation (IPPO) with RNN policies. We investigate reward shaping, particularly reward blending and post-fill markout, to mitigate credit-assignment difficulties between the agents. Our redesigned single-agent market maker quotes more frequently and incurs smaller held-out losses than the retrained JaxMARL-HFT baseline, although the contributions of jointly changed observations, actions and risk constraints are not separately identified. Decomposition alone performs poorly; careful reward design substantially improves the desk relative to the unshaped split and yields our best result. Models are evaluated on realised end-of-episode portfolio value on held-out markets. None establishes positive average portfolio value in periodic held-out evaluation, and each configuration was trained with one seed. The environment, data and protocol lay a foundation for makers that quote many linked markets at once.

infographic.key_insight: A cooperative quoter–risk-manager split achieved the best reported market-making result only with careful reward shaping; decomposition alone performed poorly.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The work provides a data-reconstruction and training pipeline for studying liquidity provision in thin prediction-market order books.
method: Reconstruct order-level LOBSTER-format data from Polymarket L2 feeds.
Redesign single-agent observations, quoting actions and inventory controls.
Train cooperative quoter and risk-manager RNN policies with recurrent IPPO, testing reward blending and post-fill markout.
infographic.evidence_signal: Training used data from 417 real markets, with held-out evaluation based on realised end-of-episode portfolio value; no configuration established positive average value in periodic evaluation.
infographic.watch_item: Each configuration used one training seed, and jointly changed observations, actions and risk constraints prevent isolating their individual contributions.
infographic.paper_title: Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Market Making on Prediction-Market Order Books

title: Trajectory Replay: Continuous-Time Mixture Transport for Lifelong Generative Models
authors: Alessandro Palma, Charles Jones, Tristan Cinquin, Fabian J. Theis, Frederik Wenkel
abstract: Adapting pre-trained continuous-time generative models to sequentially incoming data without forgetting earlier tasks is a central challenge in lifelong learning. A leading strategy, generative replay, uses a generative model trained on historical tasks to augment its own continual update with synthetic samples from experience. However, it requires full trajectory simulations at every training step, which accumulate discretization errors and can degrade the replayed historical distribution. Here, we propose trajectory replay, which bypasses sample generation by training an updated velocity field to match both a frozen historical velocity along its trajectories and the incoming task's velocity field, weighted by a stability-plasticity coefficient. Through the lens of continuous-time transport, we show the resulting optimum averages the two task velocities by their respective densities and generates the mixture of their probability paths. Combined with mean velocity distillation, trajectory replay accesses historical trajectories using only a few network evaluations per continual update. Empirically, it outperforms generative replay and distillation baselines on class-incremental image generation. In two biological case studies, trajectory replay extends generative perturbation models to new contexts and experimental batches across two data modalities while preserving treatment-effect prediction.

infographic.key_insight: Trajectory replay preserves prior tasks while learning new ones by matching historical and incoming velocity fields, yielding density-weighted transport of their probability-path mixture.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It offers a way to continually update continuous-time generative models without repeatedly simulating full historical trajectories for synthetic replay.
method: Train an updated velocity field against a frozen historical field along historical trajectories and the incoming task’s field.
Balance retention and adaptation with a stability–plasticity coefficient.
Use mean velocity distillation to access historical trajectories with only a few network evaluations per update.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports better class-incremental image generation than generative replay and distillation baselines, plus two biological case studies across two modalities that preserve treatment-effect prediction.
infographic.watch_item: Practical retention may depend on the stability–plasticity setting and the accuracy of distilled historical trajectories; the abstract provides no quantitative error or runtime results.
infographic.paper_title: Trajectory Replay: Continuous-Time Mixture Transport for Lifelong Generative Models

title: VaDar: Implicit Goal Conditioning via Value Disaggregation
authors: Shashwat Saxena, Mehul Goel, Sreyas Venkataraman, Sarvesh Patil, Max Simchowitz
abstract: Long-horizon tasks are important for modern AI and robotics, yet pose a challenge for reinforcement learning. Historically, a popular approach has been to decompose a task into subgoals, and learn a subgoal-conditioned policy to execute each subtask in sequence. We introduce an alternative called Value Disaggregation (VaDar), which trains a single subgoal-independent policy to maximize a linear combination of per-subgoal critic values. Because subgoal information is needed only at training-time, VaDar removes the need for possibly costly or cumbersome subgoal-selection during policy deployment. Moreover, through careful experiments, we show that VaDar (1) is always competitive with, and frequently outperforms, natural baselines like goal-conditioning and (2) succeeds on tasks with non-sequential goal structure and multiple optimization objectives. In particular, VaDar is the first algorithm to solve challenging, long-horizon tasks in the RoboCasa suite, even when starting from a policy pretrained from behavior cloning with near-zero initial task success. Taken together, VaDar's successes suggest that subgoal information benefits actor-critic reinforcement learning by enhancing the efficacy of critic learning, whereas policy goal-conditioning is often unnecessary.

infographic.key_insight: VaDar uses subgoal-specific critics to train one subgoal-independent policy, eliminating explicit subgoal selection at deployment.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For long-horizon robotic tasks, VaDar can simplify deployment by moving subgoal handling into training rather than requiring a runtime subgoal selector.
method: Learn per-subgoal critic values.
Train a single policy to maximize a linear combination of those values.
Deploy the policy without subgoal inputs or explicit subgoal selection.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports competitive or better performance than goal-conditioning baselines, success on non-sequential and multi-objective tasks, and the first algorithm to solve challenging long-horizon RoboCasa tasks, including from behavior-cloned policies with near-zero initial task success.
infographic.watch_item: Training still requires subgoal information and per-subgoal critics; the abstract does not quantify annotation costs or sensitivity to critic-combination weights.
infographic.paper_title: VaDar: Implicit Goal Conditioning via Value Disaggregation

title: Reinforcement Learning with Visually Attributable On-Policy Self-Distillation
authors: Shiao Xie, Siyu Chen, Jianwei Lv, Xiandong Li, Yujin Wang
abstract: Multimodal reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) provides reliable task-level supervision, yet offers limited guidance for localizing errors in visual reasoning. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) complements this supervision with dense token-level corrections from a privileged teacher equipped with an evidence-centered visual view. However, the resulting corrections may conflate visual evidence with non-visual shifts induced by linguistic priors, response style, or the privileged view itself. We formalize this phenomenon as privileged-correction contamination: a token-level correction is contaminated when its update direction cannot be consistently attributed to the privileged visual evidence. Directly distilling contaminated corrections may therefore reinforce erroneous token-level updates. To address this issue, we propose reinforcement learning with visually attributable on-policy self-distillation, an evidence-consistent paradigm that augments task-level RLVR supervision with privileged token-level corrections grounded in visual evidence. We instantiate this paradigm with Visual-Attribution Gating (VAG), which uses the verifier-derived advantage as the optimization anchor and validates each privileged correction against the contrast between evidence-present and evidence-degraded teacher views. By admitting only corrections directionally supported by this visual contrast, VAG preserves visually grounded guidance while suppressing inconsistent residuals. Experiments across six visual reasoning benchmarks show that VAG consistently outperforms GRPO and OPSD methods, establishing new state-of-the-art average performance.

infographic.key_insight: Visual-Attribution Gating (VAG) filters privileged teacher corrections to retain updates supported by visual evidence rather than non-visual influences.
infographic.engineering_relevance: VAG offers a way to combine verifiable task rewards with visually grounded token-level feedback when training multimodal reasoning models.
method: Anchor optimization with verifier-derived advantages from reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards.
Contrast evidence-present and evidence-degraded teacher views to assess visual support for each correction.
Admit directionally supported corrections and suppress inconsistent residuals during on-policy self-distillation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across six visual reasoning benchmarks, the abstract reports consistent gains over GRPO and OPSD methods and a new state-of-the-art average performance, without numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Gating reliability may depend on how evidence-degraded views are constructed; the abstract does not specify this procedure or its computational overhead.
infographic.paper_title: Reinforcement Learning with Visually Attributable On-Policy Self-Distillation

title: CoopUQ: Robust Multi-Robot Social Navigation via Uncertainty-Aware Cooperative Forecasting
authors: Zehao Wang, Jianpeng Yao, Yuping Wang, Yiping Li, Jiaqi Li, Zhixu Li
abstract: Reinforcement learning enables mobile robots to make fast and scalable navigation decisions in constrained human-shared environments. However, directly extending single-robot approaches to multi-robot settings often fails to ensure safety and efficiency, especially under occlusions and out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios, where individual robots may overlook potential risks or make inaccurate predictions. Leveraging cooperation effectively for both prediction and navigation remains a major challenge. We propose CoopUQ, a multi-robot social navigation framework that bridges uncertainty-aware cooperative occupancy forecasting and robust decision making. CoopUQ predicts future occupancy grid maps through cross-robot spatiotemporal feature fusion and further leverages forecasts and their uncertainty to guide policy via constrained multi-agent reinforcement learning, where the cost penalizes navigation through regions predicted to be occupied or highly uncertain. This design enables the policy to adapt its risk sensitivity under distribution shifts. Experimental results across multiple Unity3D-based simulation environments with both in-distribution and OOD settings, including diverse layouts, pedestrian densities, and rushing behavior, demonstrate improved prediction performance and safety over representative baselines. Real-robot experiments further demonstrate its robustness across various scenes. Our code and videos are available at https://coopuq.github.io/.

infographic.key_insight: CoopUQ improves multi-robot social navigation by combining cooperative occupancy forecasts with uncertainty-aware risk penalties.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Sharing predictive information across robots can support safer navigation around people when occlusions or unfamiliar conditions undermine individual perception.
method: Fuse spatiotemporal features across robots to forecast future occupancy grids.
Estimate forecast uncertainty alongside predicted occupancy.
Train navigation policies with constrained multi-agent reinforcement learning that penalizes occupied or highly uncertain regions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports improved prediction and safety over representative baselines in Unity3D simulations spanning in-distribution and OOD conditions, plus robustness demonstrations on real robots.
infographic.watch_item: Deployment should assess communication latency and failures, whose effects on cooperative forecasting are not specified in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: CoopUQ: Robust Multi-Robot Social Navigation via Uncertainty-Aware Cooperative Forecasting

title: Newton-Based Methods for Bilevel Optimization Beyond Lower-Level Strong Convexity
authors: Youran Dong, Junfeng Yang, Wei Yao, Jin Zhang
abstract: Bilevel optimization provides a framework for machine learning tasks such as hyperparameter optimization, data reweighting, and meta-learning. Existing Newton-based bilevel methods typically rely on the classical hypergradient formula, which is generally unavailable when lower-level solutions are nonunique and the lower-level Hessian is singular. We develop two Newton-based methods beyond lower-level strong convexity by exploiting curvature shared by the lower-level and multiplier updates. Newton-based GALET handles potentially singular lower-level curvature under a positive spectral-gap condition, exploiting its range structure to avoid the squared-Hessian multiplier system used in GALET. Newton-based BAMM uses a strongly convex aggregation model when the lower-level objective is convex and the upper-level objective is strongly convex in the lower-level variable. We establish convergence guarantees and improved complexity bounds relative to GALET and sl-BAMM under the corresponding assumptions. We further introduce GNBO, a generalized Newton-based framework that captures the shared-curvature structure of the proposed methods and several existing Newton and quasi-Newton bilevel methods. Experiments on synthetic problems, data hyper-cleaning, and GPT-2 data reweighting evaluate the proposed methods across different bilevel learning tasks.

infographic.key_insight: Shared curvature enables Newton-based bilevel optimization beyond lower-level strong convexity, including settings with nonunique solutions and singular Hessians.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The methods broaden Newton-based tools for hyperparameter optimization, data reweighting, and meta-learning when standard hypergradient assumptions fail.
method: Newton-based GALET exploits curvature range structure under a positive spectral gap, avoiding GALET’s squared-Hessian multiplier system.
Newton-based BAMM uses strongly convex aggregation when the lower-level objective is convex and the upper-level objective is strongly convex in the lower-level variable.
GNBO unifies the shared-curvature structure of the proposed methods and several existing Newton and quasi-Newton bilevel methods.
infographic.evidence_signal: The paper establishes convergence and improved complexity bounds over GALET and sl-BAMM under corresponding assumptions, and evaluates synthetic problems, data hyper-cleaning, and GPT-2 data reweighting.
infographic.watch_item: Guarantees remain conditional on spectral-gap or convexity assumptions; the abstract reports no quantitative empirical gains.
infographic.paper_title: Newton-Based Methods for Bilevel Optimization Beyond Lower-Level Strong Convexity

title: OpenVLHarness: Real World Visual Agentic Tool-Use with Multimodal Memory
authors: Yu Zhou, Cheng-Fu Yang, Rui Sun, Di Wu, Sibo Peng, Mingyang Zhang
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made rapid progress on visual reasoning, yet many tasks require evidence that is difficult to obtain through internal reasoning alone: our controlled study on 22 benchmarks shows that simply increasing the inference budget of the base model yields only modest gains. Such tasks demand grounded perception, external knowledge, and numerical measurements obtained through heterogeneous tools, whose outputs must be made interpretable to the model and retained across reasoning steps. We introduce OpenVLHarness, a multimodal reasoning harness organized around a capability layer and persistent multimodal memory. The capability layer combines task-level tool interfaces with evidence rendering, providing consistent access to heterogeneous backends and converting their outputs into model-readable observations. Persistent multimodal memory retains the corresponding images, structured data, and web references as addressable artifacts throughout each query. A coding interface executes generated programs over stored data, enabling computations that combine results from multiple tools. Together, these mechanisms support an iterative process of acquiring, inspecting, and composing multimodal evidence. Evaluated on 22 benchmarks with eight open and proprietary backbones, OpenVLHarness improves average scores by 9.7-12.6 points over matched no-tool baselines, including +11.2 with Qwen3-VL-8B, +9.7 with Kimi K3, and +9.9 with GPT-6 Astra. With GPT-6 Luna at medium reasoning effort, OpenVLHarness outperforms the base model, Codex, and Visual Sketchpad at maximum effort by 7.7-8.5 points while incurring at most 37% of their model-token cost.

infographic.key_insight: OpenVLHarness improves visual reasoning by enabling models to acquire, retain, and compute over external multimodal evidence rather than relying only on more inference.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A unified tool layer and persistent evidence store offer a reusable architecture for visual agents that combine perception, web knowledge, and numerical computation.
method: Expose heterogeneous tools through task-level interfaces and render outputs as model-readable observations.
Retain images, structured data, and web references as addressable artifacts throughout each query.
Execute generated code over stored evidence to combine tool results across reasoning steps.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 22 benchmarks and eight backbones, reported gains were 9.7–12.6 points over matched no-tool baselines; GPT-6 Luna at medium effort beat maximum-effort comparators by 7.7–8.5 points using at most 37% of their model-token cost.
infographic.watch_item: Model-token savings do not establish lower end-to-end cost or latency; tool execution, evidence storage, and generated-code safety require separate assessment.
infographic.paper_title: OpenVLHarness: Real World Visual Agentic Tool-Use with Multimodal Memory

title: Train An Imaginative Agent
authors: Jiaxin Ge, Junyi Zhang, Tianning Chai, Hanjun Yoo, Chenyang Wang, Xiuyu Li
abstract: A seemingly reasonable push in Sokoban can make the puzzle unsolvable. To avoid such mistakes, an agent has to anticipate the consequences of its actions before execution, especially when feedback from the real environment is sparse or actions are irreversible. We introduce Agentic Imagination (Agima), a training framework that trains an agent to imagine before acting, i.e. to be imaginative. Agima trains a single omni model to propose actions, generate images of their outcomes, and then reason over these imagined futures to decide what to execute in the real environment. Rather than committing to a single plan, the agent can simulate a sequence of actions, explore alternatives, and compare possible futures. We first use supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to unify policy and world modeling within a single omni model. This enables the agent to predict future outcomes and perform basic forms of imagination, such as forward thinking and counterfactual branching. We then use agentic reinforcement learning (RL) to teach the agent to reason with its imagined futures and use them effectively for planning. Across four environments spanning Maze2D, Sokoban, Pacman, and PushT, Agima generalizes to harder settings unseen during training. Trained with SFT alone on two-box Sokoban, Agima solves 40% of four-box puzzles while seeing the real board only once every five moves, compared with an action-only planner that only solves 2%. After RL, new behaviors emerge in how Agima uses its imagination: it learns a new unified format that was unseen during the SFT stage, learns to conduct forward thinking only when necessary, and branches more frequently at critical decision points. An agent that can picture where its actions lead can learn when and where to look ahead, that is, to plan. Project page: https://agima.net/.

infographic.key_insight: Agentic Imagination (Agima) trains a single model to propose actions, visualize their consequences, and reason over imagined futures before acting.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Imagined rollouts could support planning when real-world feedback is sparse or actions are difficult to reverse.
method: Use supervised fine-tuning to unify action selection and image-based world modeling in one omni model.
Simulate action sequences and branch into alternatives to compare possible futures.
Apply agentic reinforcement learning to learn when and where imagination helps planning.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across Maze2D, Sokoban, Pacman, and PushT, Agima generalizes to harder unseen settings; SFT-only training on two-box Sokoban yields 40% success on four-box puzzles versus 2% for an action-only planner, with real-board observations every five moves.
infographic.watch_item: Evaluation covers four environments; transfer to real-world tasks and robustness to errors in imagined outcomes remain unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Train An Imaginative Agent

title: On Data Scaling in Tabular ML: More Data, Better Generalization?
authors: Ivan Rubachev, Nikita Lazarev, Artem Babenko
abstract: Recent work in tabular machine learning has emphasized the importance of diverse and realistic evaluation settings. The niche of large-scale (1M+) data, however, remains under-explored. To study training-data scaling, we assemble eight real-world tabular datasets with up to around ten million training examples, retaining the natural distribution shifts of the tasks and using random-split evaluation as a control. We find that GBDTs and MLP-based models show broadly similar scaling trends, with gains from both additional training data and algorithmic improvements. Tabular foundation models show more varied scaling behavior, with recent versions benefiting more consistently from larger contexts even under distribution shift. However, scaling training data under distribution shift introduces new challenges: in-distribution and out-of-distribution performance mostly improve together at smaller scales but can diverge at larger scales. We examine this through MLP capacity sweeps and comparisons of the validation distributions used for tuning and early stopping in MLPs and GBDTs. We also compare common practices of using validation data, contrasting its use for model selection in MLP pipelines with using it for in-context fitting in tabular foundation model pipelines. Under stronger shifts, MLPs selected using validation representative of the evaluation conditions generally maintain or improve performance as training data grows. In contrast, including such examples in context improves foundation-model performance, but does not prevent deterioration with increasing training size in our experiments.

infographic.key_insight: More training data often improves tabular models, but under distribution shift, in-distribution gains can diverge from out-of-distribution performance at larger scales.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For deployment under distribution shift, scale training data alongside evaluation-representative validation rather than assuming larger datasets guarantee better generalization.
method: Study training-data scaling across eight real-world tabular datasets, preserving natural shifts and using random splits as controls.
Compare GBDTs, MLP-based models, and tabular foundation models across data scales.
Examine MLP capacity, validation distributions for tuning and early stopping, and foundation-model context composition.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across datasets with up to around 10 million training examples, GBDTs and MLPs show broadly similar scaling trends, while foundation-model behavior is more varied.
infographic.watch_item: Under stronger shifts, adding evaluation-representative examples to foundation-model contexts improves performance but does not prevent deterioration as training size grows in these experiments.
infographic.paper_title: On Data Scaling in Tabular ML: More Data, Better Generalization?

title: recAMPLIFY: Large-Scale Pretraining of Recursive Protein Language Models
authors: Saurav Jha, Qianli Liao, Robert Vernon, Sarath Chandar, Quentin Fournier
abstract: Protein language models (pLMs) are powerful tools for protein annotation and mutation-effect prediction, but progress has largely depended on scaling model size and data, making them expensive and prone to memorization. Test-time scaling offers a complementary path, but methods developed for autoregressive LLMs do not transfer directly: masked encoders lack a generation loop, and amino acids do not verbalize in a reasoning language. Instead, we adapt recursive pretraining to masked pLMs, where a weight-tied Transformer core refines residue-aligned hidden states over an adjustable number of cycles. We instantiate this recipe as recAMPLIFY, a pLM with 155M unique parameters trained on the same 2T tokens as AMPLIFY-350M. Despite 56% fewer parameters, it improves CASP contact recovery and three out of four supervised tasks, notably raising fold accuracy by 22.5%. Because optimal depth for recAMPLIFY varies across tasks and assays, we then introduce Gated Mixture Recurrence (GMR), a framework that decodes each protein from a probability-weighted mixture of hidden states visited during recursion. GMR employs a learned residual gate at scalar, low-rank, or per-dimension resolution to control how much of each cycle's proposed update is accepted into the state. This unifies halting and gating into a single adaptive computation objective while recovering PonderNet-style halting as a special case without gates. Layered on top of recAMPLIFY, GMR further reduces expected layer depth by up to 37%, although the accuracy trade-off varies by task. Mechanistic analyses show that residual gating controls recurrence stability beyond the trained depth and that halt depth tracks biological properties.

infographic.key_insight: recAMPLIFY reuses a weight-tied Transformer core to improve protein predictions with 56% fewer unique parameters than AMPLIFY-350M.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Adjustable recurrence offers a way to trade inference compute for predictive quality without increasing unique parameter count.
method: Recursively refine residue-aligned hidden states in a masked protein language model.
Use Gated Mixture Recurrence to decode a probability-weighted mixture of states across cycles.
Learn residual gates that control how much each cycle updates the hidden state.
infographic.evidence_signal: With 155M unique parameters and the same 2T training tokens as AMPLIFY-350M, recAMPLIFY improves CASP contact recovery and 3 of 4 supervised tasks, including a reported 22.5% increase in fold accuracy.
infographic.watch_item: Optimal recurrence depth varies by task and assay; GMR reduces expected layer depth by up to 37%, but accuracy trade-offs are task-dependent.
infographic.paper_title: recAMPLIFY: Large-Scale Pretraining of Recursive Protein Language Models

title: Copying Under Repetition: From Prefix Matching to Position Hashing
authors: Anxin Guo, Tianlong Huang, Chenxiao Yang, Zhiyuan Li
abstract: Frontier LLMs can copy random text almost flawlessly, yet they often overrun or truncate long blocks of repeated characters. In repeated strings, matching local content no longer reliably identifies where copying should continue or when it should stop. Nevertheless, we show that a two-layer transformer with $O(\log\log N)$-bit precision and $O(\log N/\log\log N)$ width can copy every string up to a chosen design horizon $N$ and terminate correctly under arbitrary repetition. We use RoPE-style rotations of attention values and outputs (VO-rotations) with small prime periods to encode distances from delimiter anchors modulo those primes. By the Chinese Remainder Theorem, these periodic encodings jointly distinguish all required distances, allowing one retrieval rule to select either the next source token or the end marker. In contrast, we prove a width-independent impossibility result for copying under sequential finite-precision softmax accumulation. It applies to transformers whose only positional input is an additive attention bias that eventually becomes constant, including NoPE and a recursive implementation of ALiBi. Once an identical-token run exceeds the resulting saturation threshold, further repetitions leave the logits unchanged. If this threshold grows sublinearly with $N$, these models cannot both complete a long all-identical copy and stop correctly, a pattern resembling the termination errors of frontier LLMs. In synthetic copying experiments, baseline transformer models fail on long repeated strings even within the training range. Trained VO models, by contrast, generalize beyond the training lengths with near-perfect accuracy up to length $\approx 5005$, the selected primes' period product.

infographic.key_insight: Repeated text defeats content-based copying, but a compact two-layer transformer can copy and stop correctly by encoding positions as modular distances from delimiter anchors.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Position-aware retrieval offers a route to more reliable exact copying and termination when repeated content makes local token matches ambiguous.
method: Apply RoPE-style rotations to attention values and outputs using small prime periods.
Combine modular distances via the Chinese Remainder Theorem to retrieve the next token or end marker.
Prove a copying impossibility result under sequential finite-precision softmax accumulation for positional biases that eventually become constant.
infographic.evidence_signal: In synthetic copying experiments, baselines failed on long repeated strings even within training lengths, while trained VO models generalized beyond training with near-perfect accuracy up to approximately 5005 tokens, the selected primes' period product.
infographic.watch_item: The guarantee is bounded by a chosen design horizon, and synthetic copying results do not establish reliability in general-purpose LLM deployments.
infographic.paper_title: Copying Under Repetition: From Prefix Matching to Position Hashing

title: AllPath: Layered Verification for a Deployed, Self-Revising LLM Trading Agent under Human-Gated and Autonomous Regimes
authors: Tian Zhang, Meng Li
abstract: LLM trading agents are evaluated almost exclusively in backtests and autonomous benchmark harnesses. Deployment, where actions are irreversible, raises a different question: who verifies the agent's actions, and which failures can each verifier structurally catch? We report on AllPath, a personal LLM trading agent deployed against a live paper-brokerage account. The system watches positions through a deterministic rules engine, and each night it reviews its own day and proposes revisions to its own trading strategies. Verification is split across three layers. Code verifies what must not depend on judgment: deterministic gates enforce risk limits and block any strategy revision that fails an integrity check. The agent verifies itself within fixed bounds: its nightly review has an iteration cap and no tools that can act. A human verifies judgment, through approval screens that show the current state of each proposal. We also compared two verification policies for the agent's self-revisions on the live system: two and a half weeks with every self-revision human-gated, then five weeks with reflection revisions auto-applied behind the same code gates, while the operator's chat channel stayed human-gated throughout. Each layer caught a different kind of failure. The code gates rejected no proposal; their role was keeping revisions consistent. The human rejected two proposals that passed every code check, both over a disagreement about the market, and later removed 11 of the 19 rules the agent had added on its own, at a median lag of eight days. The most instructive production incidents, such as strategies silently left unmonitored, passed every gate; the operator found them by hand, and the fix each time was an interface change that makes the condition visible. We contribute the layered architecture, the two-regime account, and a production incident taxonomy, none observable in a backtest.

infographic.key_insight: Layered verification catches different failures, but code-valid trading revisions can still conflict with human judgment or leave operational blind spots.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Deployed self-revising agents need deterministic safeguards, bounded reflection, human oversight, and interfaces that expose failures beyond gate checks.
method: Deployed an LLM trading agent against a live paper-brokerage account with nightly strategy self-revisions.
Combined deterministic risk and revision-integrity gates, bounded tool-restricted review, and human approval screens.
Compared 2.5 weeks of human-gated self-revisions with 5 weeks of auto-applied reflection revisions; chat remained human-gated.
infographic.evidence_signal: Code gates rejected no proposals; the human rejected two code-valid proposals and later removed 11 of 19 autonomously added rules at a median lag of eight days, while manually discovering incidents that passed every gate.
infographic.watch_item: This sequential, single-agent paper-trading deployment does not establish real-money safety or a causal advantage for either verification regime.
infographic.paper_title: AllPath: Layered Verification for a Deployed, Self-Revising LLM Trading Agent under Human-Gated and Autonomous Regimes

title: WhatIf-Bench: Benchmarking Intervention-Aware Time Series Forecasting
authors: Arjun Ashok, Mihir Parmar, Palash Goyal, Bhavana Dalvi Mishra, Chun-Liang Li, Irina Rish
abstract: Recent time series foundation models (TSFMs) can consume covariates in-context, extending zero-shot forecasting to problems driven by external factors. This enables scenario analysis: forecasting how a target responds to events that set covariates to chosen future values. Whether they can do this reliably is an open question. We introduce WhatIf-Bench, a benchmark measuring how well forecasters use covariates to forecast a target's response to future events. WhatIf-Bench is semi-synthetic: time series come from mechanistic simulators of data centers, power grids, road traffic, and water networks, with controlled covariate-target relationships grounded in each system. Each task presents a history of events intervening on covariates, then asks to forecast a future event that either replays seen values (Replay) or sets them to unseen ones (Novel). Varying the number of covariates, historical events, and event length yields 37,665 tasks. Evaluating TSFMs, frontier LLMs, and simple regression baselines, we find the LLMs reach the highest skill (improvement over a naive baseline), ahead of the best TSFMs. Every model forecasts well on Replay futures (48 to 85% skill) but drops to -7 to 50% on Novel futures, with the regression baselines falling the most. Skill on Novel futures also falls as events set more covariates jointly. More historical events raise skill on Novel futures across the board, but large differences remain. WhatIf-Bench reveals generalization to Novel futures as the core challenge, and offers a testbed toward arbitrary scenario analysis.

infographic.key_insight: Forecasting models handle familiar intervention values well but struggle with unseen values, making novel scenario generalization the central challenge.
infographic.engineering_relevance: WhatIf-Bench tests whether forecasters can support what-if planning in data centers, power grids, road traffic, and water networks.
method: Generate semi-synthetic time series using mechanistic simulators with controlled covariate–target relationships.
Forecast future interventions that reuse historical covariate values (Replay) or introduce unseen values (Novel).
Vary covariate count, historical event count, and event length; compare TSFMs, frontier LLMs, and regression baselines.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 37,665 tasks, skill relative to a naive baseline ranges from 48–85% on Replay to −7–50% on Novel futures, with frontier LLMs achieving the highest skill.
infographic.watch_item: The benchmark is semi-synthetic, so performance does not establish reliability for real-world interventions beyond the simulated systems.
infographic.paper_title: WhatIf-Bench: Benchmarking Intervention-Aware Time Series Forecasting

title: BetaMem: Learning to Remember a Changing World for Embodied Agents
authors: Mai Liu, He Sun, Siru Zhong, Kerun Chen, Hao Yan, Xiaohui Lv
abstract: Long-horizon embodied agents face temporal confusion and incomplete or distorted records, recurring errors from fixed memory rules, and growing storage and retrieval costs. We present BetaMem, a framework for building and evolving traceable long-term memory through six linked layers: working, spatial, entity, episodic, experiential, and procedural memory. A dual-level write contract constrains operation executability and source support for content: supervised fine-tuning learns compliant memory operations, while reinforcement learning combines repeated sampling with teacher verification of the original observations to reward complete, accurate records and penalize omissions, distortion, and unsupported content. We formulate failure-driven policy recursive self-improvement through diagnosis along the causal sequence of memory operations and local rule repairs gated by independent replay. Atomic tools frame storage, updates, retrieval, and forgetting as cost-utility allocation under storage and read budgets. Using the open-source Qwen3.5-9B model for memory generation, BetaMem achieves overall scores of 48.08% on M3-Bench-robot, 92.08% on LoCoMo, 72.6% on OpenEQA EM-EQA, and 62.4% on EgoLifeQA, the highest among the listed memory methods under their respective evaluation protocols. Training the model for memory generation raises the contract pass rate from 50.9% to 86.2% while reducing output tokens per stored action by 47.3%. A separate Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct evaluation on EMem-Bench achieves an average success rate of 38.4% and an average error recurrence rate of 24.9%. We perform best among evaluated methods using comparably sized open-source models. Category results show that we have advantages in integrating information across observations, recalling events over long histories, and inferring personal habits.

infographic.key_insight: BetaMem gives embodied agents traceable, evolving long-term memory by combining grounded memory writing, failure-driven rule repair, and budget-aware storage and retrieval.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework targets more reliable long-horizon agents while controlling memory growth, retrieval costs, and repeated mistakes.
method: Links six memory layers: working, spatial, entity, episodic, experiential, and procedural.
Uses supervised fine-tuning and teacher-verified reinforcement learning to enforce executable, source-supported memory writes.
Repairs memory policies through causal failure diagnosis and independent replay checks, with budget-aware tools for storage, updates, retrieval, and forgetting.
infographic.evidence_signal: With Qwen3.5-9B, BetaMem reports leading scores among listed memory methods on four benchmarks; training raises write-contract compliance from 50.9% to 86.2% and reduces output tokens per stored action by 47.3%.
infographic.watch_item: Results use benchmark-specific evaluation protocols, and teacher verification plus replay checks may add implementation and compute overhead.
infographic.paper_title: BetaMem: Learning to Remember a Changing World for Embodied Agents

title: Agentic Orchestration of EDC Data Space Retrieval and Natural Language Driven Data Processing
authors: Marla Grunewald, Fin Gentzen, Iulisloi Zacarias, Admela Jukan
abstract: Participating in a data space still requires the Dataspace Protocol (DSP) negotiation flow to be hand-coded against each provider's access policy. We present a multi-agent architecture that automates this process using natural language requests. Built on LangGraph over an Eclipse Dataspace Components (EDC), the design separates concerns into cooperating agents. The orchestrator's role is to route and plan. The data extraction agent's role is to expose the DSP protocol's three composable tools (catalog discovery, contract negotiation and download). The agent also gates negotiations on the consumers' verifiable credentials, refusing assets rather than fabricating them. Furthermore, there are downstream Machine Learning (ML) and Visualization agents, as well as a final Verification agent, which confirms that the request was actually fulfilled and rechecks the intended operation against the contract's usage policy. In a primary benchmark involving 600 runs, the system achieved 89% task success with zero policy violations when evaluating multi-dimensional policy reasoning with a locally hosted open-weight model. It failed safely through refusal rather than misrouting. The reliability of the system is largely dependent on the phrasing of requests: technical and expert requests succeed up to 98% of the time, whereas casual and under-specified requests succeed 72% of the time. Furthermore, in a secondary evaluation of 600 runs isolating hierarchical geographic access control, the framework successfully blocks 100% of unauthorized regional requests. While the verification agent hallucinates that 1% of these requests, the system logs confirm that no data is ever extracted and the framework simultaneously achieves an end-to-end verified delivery rate of 86% for eligible consumers.

infographic.key_insight: A multi-agent system turns natural-language requests into policy-aware data retrieval and processing, achieving 89% task success with zero observed policy violations in its primary benchmark.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The architecture offers a way to automate data-space access workflows while checking consumer credentials and contract usage policies.
method: Use LangGraph to orchestrate specialized agents over Eclipse Dataspace Components (EDC).
Expose catalog discovery, contract negotiation and download as tools, gating negotiation on verifiable credentials.
Route downstream work to ML and visualization agents, then verify fulfillment and usage-policy compliance.
infographic.evidence_signal: Two 600-run evaluations reported 89% primary task success and, in a separate geographic-access test, 100% blocking of unauthorized requests with 86% verified delivery for eligible consumers.
infographic.watch_item: Reliability depends on request phrasing: success ranged from 72% for casual, underspecified requests to 98% for technical requests; verification also hallucinated fulfillment for 1% of unauthorized regional requests despite no logged extraction.
infographic.paper_title: Agentic Orchestration of EDC Data Space Retrieval and Natural Language Driven Data Processing
